title: Japan's Asuka-Fujiwara Sites Added to UNESCO List
paragraphs: Nestled among the pastoral fields of the Nara Basin, a collection of ancient palace ruins, temples and burial mounds has gained international recognition as the birthplace of the Japanese state. On July 26, 2026, the "Ancient Capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara" were inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee, held in Busan, South Korea. According to the Japanese government, the property is Japan's 27th World Heritage site.

The inscription recognizes the pivotal role that the region played during the Asuka period, which spanned from 592 to 710. During this era, Japan underwent a profound transformation from a loose federation of powerful clans into a centralized state headed by the emperor. Drawing heavily on Chinese models, rulers introduced legal codes, administrative structures and systems of taxation, while Buddhism became a central element of statecraft. It was also during this period that the name by which Japan is known today was established.

From 630, the Asuka Palace served as the nation's political and cultural center for more than six decades. It was there, in 645, that a dramatic coup known as the Isshi Incident wrested power from the dominant Soga clan and restored it to the imperial court. Subsequently, in 694, Fujiwarakyo was completed. As Japan's first fully planned capital, laid out on a grid covering an area of roughly five kilometers square, it was designed to govern a centralized state according to the ritsuryo legal codes, and its design later served as the model for the capitals of Nara and Kyoto.

The property encompasses a remarkable variety of sites. Among the most striking is the Ishibutai Mounded Tomb, whose exposed stone chamber is constructed from approximately 30 boulders with an estimated combined weight of 2,300 tons. It is believed to be the tomb of Soga no Umako, a powerful statesman of the era. Equally significant are the Takamatsuzuka and Kitora tombs, whose multicolored murals are the only surviving examples of their kind in Japan and have been designated national treasures. The site also includes the remains of Japan's oldest water clock, built in 660.

Other components include the ruins of the Fujiwara Palace, the Asuka water clock and ritual sites, and early Buddhist temples such as Motoyakushiji and Kawaradera. Local authorities hope that World Heritage status will encourage more people to explore this quiet rural landscape.
